title: Assignment: binary tree problems from level-order input
overview: This is the binary tree assignment. Every program first builds a tree from **level-order input** (`-1` means no child), then answers one question: sum of non-leaf nodes, leaves in descending order, is the tree perfect, the nodes on level X, and the outer side of the tree. Revising it is a good way to practise the two tools you use for every tree problem: BFS with a queue and recursive DFS.

concepts.term: Building a tree from level order
concepts.explain: Read the root, push it into a queue, then for each popped node read two numbers: its left and right child (`-1` = none). New children are pushed so their children are read later, in the same order.
concepts.snippet:
cin >> l >> r;
p->left = (l == -1) ? NULL : new Node(l);

concepts.explain: A leaf has no children (`!left && !right`). An internal node has at least one child. Many questions just filter on this test.
`count(root) = count(left) + count(right) + 1` and `depth(root) = max(depth(left), depth(right)) + 1`, both with 0 for NULL.
A tree of depth d (root at depth 1) is perfect exactly when it has 2^d - 1 nodes, because every level is completely full.
Store `{node, level}` in the queue to know each node's level, then collect nodes whose level equals X.
Walk down the left edge (go left if possible, else right) and print it bottom-up, print the root, then walk down the right edge (go right if possible, else left) top-down.

files.title: Sum without leaf
files.what: Builds the tree from level-order input and adds up the values of all nodes that have at least one child.
steps: `input_tree()` reads the root, then uses a queue to read two children for every node (`-1` means none).
`sum_without_leaf` runs a BFS starting at the root.
For each popped `parent`, if `parent->left || parent->right` it is not a leaf, so add `parent->val` to `sum`.
Push the existing children and keep going until the queue is empty.
`main` prints the sum.
files.input_note: Tree in level order: 10 has children 20 and 30; 20 has 40 and 50; 30 has only a right child 60; the four leaves have `-1 -1`.
files.output_note: Prints `60`: the internal nodes are 10, 20 and 30, and 10 + 20 + 30 = 60. The leaves 40, 50, 60 are skipped.
files.watch_out: An empty tree (input `-1`) returns 0 thanks to the `if(!root)` check at the top.

check.q: With the same input, what would the sum of only the leaves be?

files.title: Leaf nodes in descending order
files.what: Collects every leaf value with a recursive DFS, sorts them from largest to smallest and prints them.
steps: Build the tree with `input_tree()`.
`all_leaf_nodes(root, v)` returns on NULL; if the node has no children it pushes `root->val` into `v`.
It then recurses into the left and right subtrees (the vector is shared by reference).
`sort(ans.begin(), ans.end(), greater<int>())` puts the values in descending order.
Print them separated by spaces.
files.complexity: Time O(n + k log k) for k leaves · Space O(n)
files.input_note: Same tree as problem 1: leaves are 40, 50, 60.
files.output_note: Prints `60 50 40 ` (with a trailing space): the leaves found left to right are 40 50 60, then sorted in descending order.
files.watch_out: The function returns the vector by value while also filling it by reference, so the return value is a copy. It works, but `void` plus the reference would be enough.

check.a: It sorts in descending order instead of the default ascending order.

files.title: Is the tree perfect?
files.what: Counts the nodes and measures the depth, then checks the formula nodes = 2^depth - 1.
steps: Build the tree with `input_tree()`.
`count_nodes` returns `l + r + 1` recursively (0 for NULL).
`max_depth` returns `max(l, r) + 1` recursively (0 for NULL).
`is_perfect` computes `pow(2, depth) - 1` and compares it with the node count.
`main` prints `YES` or `NO`.
files.input_note: A full tree of depth 3: root 10, then 20 30, then 40 50 60 70, and eight `-1` for the leaves' children.
files.output_note: Prints `YES`: there are 7 nodes and the depth is 3, and 2^3 - 1 = 7. Try `10 20 30 40 -1 60 -1 -1 -1 -1 -1` and you get `NO` (5 nodes, but depth 3 needs 7).
files.watch_out: `pow` works with `double`; for large depths the result may be slightly off when converted to `int`. `(1 << depth) - 1` is exact for integers (and a perfect tree with up to 10^5 nodes has depth at most 17).

check.q: How many nodes does a perfect binary tree of depth 4 have?

files.title: Nodes on level X
files.what: Prints, from left to right, all node values on level X (root is level 0), or `Invalid` if that level does not exist.
steps: Build the tree, then read `X`.
`level_nodes` does a BFS with `{node, level}` pairs, starting at `{root, 0}`.
Every popped node whose `level == X` is added to `ans`; children get `level + 1`.
If nothing was collected, the function puts the marker `-999` in `ans`.
`main` prints `Invalid` when it sees that marker, otherwise prints the values.
files.input_note: The tree from problem 1, then X = 2 on its own line.
files.output_note: Prints `40 50 60 `: level 0 is 10, level 1 is 20 30, level 2 is 40 50 60. With X = 3 it prints `Invalid`.
files.watch_out: The BFS keeps going after level X is finished. You can stop as soon as you pop a node with `level > X` to save time. Also, `-999` works as a marker only because node values are at least 1.

check.q: Why does BFS print the level's nodes from left to right?
check.a: Children are pushed left before right, so within a level the queue holds nodes in left-to-right order.

files.title: Print the outer side of the tree (working)
files.what: Prints the left edge of the tree from bottom to top, then the root, then the right edge from top to bottom. This is the version that gives the expected answers.
steps: Build the tree with `input_tree()` (line breaks in the input do not matter to `cin`).
`left_boundary(root->left, v)` goes left if it can, otherwise right, and pushes each value **after** the recursive call, so the deepest node is stored first (bottom-up).
Push the root's value.
`right_boundary(root->right, v)` pushes each value **before** recursing, going right if it can, otherwise left, so it is stored top-down.
`print_boundary` prints the whole vector.
files.input_note: Level order: 10; its children 20 30; 20 has 40 and 70, 30 has only 50 on the right; 40 has 90 and 110, 70 none, 50 has 80 and 60; 80 has a left child 100.
files.output_note: Prints `90 40 20 10 30 50 60 `: the left edge 20 → 40 → 90 printed bottom-up, then 10, then the right edge 30 → 50 → 60.
files.watch_out: It assumes the tree is not empty: with input `-1` the root is NULL and `root->left` crashes. Add `if(root == NULL) return;` at the start of `print_boundary`.

check.q: Why does `left_boundary` push the value after the recursive call?
check.a: So the deepest node is added first, which prints the left edge from bottom to top.

files.title: Outer side as a classic boundary traversal (wrong for this problem)
files.what: An attempt using the textbook "boundary traversal": left boundary, all leaves, right boundary. That is a different problem, so the output does not match what this assignment asks.
steps: `isLeaf` tests for a node with no children.
`leftBoundaryNodes` collects the left edge top-down, skipping the leaf at the bottom.
`leafNodes` collects every leaf in the tree from left to right.
`rightBoundaryNodes` collects the right edge, skipping its leaf, in bottom-up order.
`printBoundary` prints the leaves reversed, the left edge reversed, the root, and the right edge.
files.input_note: Same tree as the working version.
files.output_note: Prints `60 100 70 110 90 40 20 10 50 30`, but the expected answer is `90 40 20 10 30 50 60`. It prints every leaf (60, 100, 70, 110, 90), not only the two edge ends, and the right edge comes out as 50 30 instead of 30 50.
files.watch_out: Wrong answer. This problem only wants the left chain and the right chain, not all leaves. Fix: drop `leafNodes`, push each left-edge node after its recursive call and each right-edge node before its recursive call (including the leaf at each end), as in `assignment_problem_5_print_order_tree_another.cpp`.

check.q: What is the difference between a "boundary traversal" and this problem's "outer side"?
check.a: Boundary traversal includes every leaf of the tree; the outer side only includes nodes on the left and right edges.

files.title: Outer side using levels (crashes)
files.what: An earlier attempt: collect all levels with repeated BFS, then take the first node of each level bottom-up and the last node of each level top-down. It crashes and the idea is also not correct in general.
steps: `level_nodes(root, X)` (from problem 4) returns the nodes of one level, or `-999`.
`all_nodes_at_all_levels` calls it for level 0, 1, 2, ... until it gets `-999`, storing each level.
`print_outer_nodes` loops `for(size_t i = levels.size()-1; i >= 0; i--)` to take the first node of every level from the bottom up.
It then takes the last node of each level (if the level has more than one node) from the top down.
`main` also reads an extra number `X` that is never used.
files.input_note: Same tree, plus a dummy `0` for the unused `X`.
files.output_note: Nothing is printed: the program crashes with an access violation (exit code `0xc0000005`).
files.watch_out: `size_t` is unsigned, so `i >= 0` is always true: after `i = 0`, `i--` wraps around to a huge number and `levels[i]` reads far outside the vector. Fix the loop with `for(int i = levels.size()-1; i >= 0; i--)`. Even then, "first/last node of each level" is not the same as the edge chain (100 on level 4 would be taken as a left-edge node), so use the approach in `assignment_problem_5_print_order_tree_another.cpp`.

check.q: Why is `for(size_t i = n-1; i >= 0; i--)` an infinite loop?
check.a: `size_t` cannot be negative; decrementing 0 wraps to the largest value, so `i >= 0` never becomes false.

recap: Level-order input: pop a node, read two numbers, `-1` means no child, push the real children.
Need levels? Put `{node, level}` pairs in the BFS queue.
Outer side: left edge bottom-up (push after recursion), root, right edge top-down (push before recursion).
Never count down with `size_t` and `i >= 0`; use a signed `int`.

check_yourself.q: For input `5 3 8 -1 -1 -1 -1`, what does problem 1 print and what does problem 2 print?
check_yourself.a: Problem 1 prints 5 (only the root has children). Problem 2 prints `8 3`.
No. It has depth 2, so a perfect tree would need 3 nodes, but it has 2.

check_yourself.q: In the level-order input, how many numbers follow the root value for a tree with n nodes?
check_yourself.a: 2n numbers: one pair (left, right) for every node, using -1 for missing children.

body: Five problems, and every one of them begins the same way: a run of numbers comes in, you turn it into a real tree, and only then answer the question. So the first tool of the day is the reader itself, the one from Module 18.

Read the first number as the root and push it into a queue. Then pop a node and read the next two numbers as its left and right child, where `-1` means no child, pushing the real children so that their children are read later. Here is the line the assignment uses and the tree it describes:

Read the numbers in pairs after the root and it is easy to follow: `20 30` are the children of 10, `40 50` the children of 20, `-1 60` says 30 has no left child and 60 on the right, and the last three pairs are the `-1 -1` of the leaves 40, 50 and 60.

Watch the edges here more than anywhere else. An empty tree is the single number `-1`, and the builder must return NULL without reading anything further. A one-node tree is `5 -1 -1`. Every node that comes off the queue reads exactly two numbers, leaves included, so input that is one pair short leaves `cin` waiting and the program looks like it has hung.

The second tool is the leaf test, `!node->left && !node->right`. Two problems are only a filter on it: problem 1 adds up the nodes that are **not** leaves, here 10 + 20 + 30 = 60, and problem 2 collects the leaves and prints them largest first, `60 50 40`.

The third tool is the pair of recursions from Module 18, both stopping at NULL: `count(root) = count(left) + count(right) + 1`, which gives 6 here, and `depth(root) = max(depth(left), depth(right)) + 1`, which gives 3 with the root at depth 1. Problem 3 uses both at once: a perfect tree has every level completely full, and a full tree of depth `d` holds exactly `2^d - 1` nodes. Here 6 is not `2^3 - 1 = 7`, so the answer is NO, and the missing left child of 30 is the gap.
The fourth tool is Module 19's queue of `{node, level}` pairs, used whenever the question mentions a level. Problem 4 reads the tree, then a number X, and prints the nodes on level X.

This assignment counts the root as level 0. Other judges start at 1, so read the samples before you trust a level number. If nothing was collected the level does not exist and the answer is the word `Invalid` rather than an empty line.

The fifth tool is a walk rather than a traversal. For the outer side of the tree you go down the left edge, taking the left child when there is one and the right child otherwise, and print that chain from the bottom up; then the root; then the right edge from the top down. On the tree above that is `40 20 10 30 60`.

Three attempts at this one are on the page, and the two failures are the useful part. One solves the textbook boundary traversal, which prints every leaf in the middle and answers a different question. The other reads collected levels backwards with an unsigned index and `i >= 0`, a test that is never false, so the index wraps round to a huge number and the program crashes. Count down with a plain `int`.

Nothing here is new: it is Module 18's builder and counts and Module 19's two shapes, used five times in a row. The programs below give each problem with its input, its output and the traps inside it.
